Four connected commercial functions. One operating point of view.

StrategyGrowthDistributionRevenue
StrategyBy lowob · 2 February 2026 · 3-minute read

You don't have three problems

Strategy

In short: fundraising, community and customer acquisition are three outputs of one commercial system. Teams that run them as separate projects pay for the same work three times and still end up with a story nobody believes.

Key points

  • A named buyer with a budget and reason to act comes first, not a market size.
  • Early evidence from that buyer, such as a pilot or letter of intent, is what the round is priced on.
  • Community is where you manufacture that evidence cheaply through testers, contributors and referrers.
  • Most teams raise on narrative and spend on distribution before finding the buyer.
  • Run one product truth, one evidence log, one calendar and one owner.

Why it splits

It splits because each one has a different audience and a different scoreboard. Investors want a market and a team. Communities want something to belong to. Customers want a problem solved. So founders write three stories.

In web3 the split is worse, because the token often makes the investor, the community member and the customer the same person. In AI the split shows up differently: the investor story is about the model or the data, while the customer only cares whether the thing works on Tuesday.

Either way, you end up with a pitch deck that promises a market, a community that has been promised a token or a feature, and a customer pipeline that hasn't heard either promise.

The dependency nobody draws

The three are not parallel. They depend on each other in a specific order.

  1. A named buyer comes first. Not a market size, a person with a budget and a reason to act now.
  2. Early evidence from that buyer — a pilot, a design partner, a letter of intent, a usage curve — is what the round is actually priced on.
  3. The community is where you manufacture that evidence cheaply: testers, contributors, referrers, the first public advocates.
  4. The round funds the distribution that turns early evidence into repeatable revenue.

Most teams try to run step 4 first. They raise on narrative, spend on distribution, and then go looking for the buyer the money was supposed to reach.

What it looks like when it goes wrong

Two patterns come up again and again.

A crypto lending product ships a dozen new markets in a month. The product objection disappears overnight. The deposits don't move. Every problem left is downstream of distribution, and none of the three workstreams was pointed at it.

An AI product has the opposite problem: real usage, happy customers, and a fundraising story about the model rather than the customers. Investors keep asking for the thing the team already has, because the deck doesn't lead with it.

Same mistake in both. The story for one audience was built without the evidence from the other two.

What changes when you run it as one system

  • One product truth. A single sentence about what this is and who buys it. Each audience gets its own belief to hold, but they all derive from the same truth.
  • One evidence log. Every pilot, quote, usage number and community contribution goes in one place, because every audience needs some of it.
  • One calendar. The raise, the community moments and the customer pushes are sequenced against each other, not run on three clocks.
  • One owner. Someone owns the order, even if three people do the work.

The checklist

  • [ ] Can you name the buyer, not the market?
  • [ ] Is there one sentence that all three audiences could repeat back?
  • [ ] Does your deck lead with the best evidence your customers and community have produced?
  • [ ] Does your community have a job beyond waiting for news?
  • [ ] Do you know what the first $100K after the round buys?

Common questions

Should fundraising, community and sales be run separately at a startup?

No. They are three outputs of one commercial system, and running them as separate projects means paying for the same work three times.

What comes first: fundraising, community or customers?

A named buyer comes first, then early evidence from that buyer, which the community helps produce cheaply. The round then funds the distribution that turns evidence into repeatable revenue.

Why is the story harder to align in Web3?

Because the token often makes the investor, the community member and the customer the same person.

What should a startup pitch deck lead with?

The best evidence your customers and community have produced, such as pilots, design partners, letters of intent or usage curves.
